back: A map with lines joining places of equal value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What are isolines of equal pressure called?
back: Isobars
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What are isolines of equal temperature called?
back: Isotherms
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What kind of data does an isoline map need?
back: Continuous data that changes gradually across space
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: Give one limitation of an isoline map.
back: Lines are estimated between data points, so they are inaccurate where points are few
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What is a dot map?
back: A map where each dot represents a fixed quantity
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: Give one strength of a dot map.
back: It shows distribution and density clearly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: Give one limitation of a dot map.
back: Dots merge in dense areas so they are hard to count
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What is a flow-line map?
back: A map with lines along routes, their width proportional to the amount of movement
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What is a desire-line map?
back: Straight lines from origin to destination showing movement, not the actual route
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What is a proportional symbol map?
back: A map with symbols whose size is proportional to the value at each place
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: For proportional circles, what is made proportional to the value?
back: The area of the circle
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: Give one limitation of proportional symbols.
back: Large symbols overlap and hide each other or the map
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What is a located graph?
back: A graph placed on a map at the location its data refer to
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What is a synoptic chart?
back: A weather map showing pressure, fronts and weather at one time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: On a synoptic chart, what do closely spaced isobars show?
back: Strong winds
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: On a synoptic chart, what is shown by isobars around low pressure?
back: A depression
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: On a synoptic chart, what is shown by isobars around high pressure?
back: An anticyclone
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: What is an atlas map?
back: A small-scale map showing patterns over large areas, such as countries
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.2 Cartographic skills

front: Which graph type shows continuous change over time?
back: A line graph
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What is a compound line graph?
back: Lines stacked so each band shows one part and the top line shows the total
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What is a comparative bar graph?
back: Bars for two or more data sets drawn side by side to compare
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What is a compound (divided) bar graph?
back: A bar split into parts that make up the total
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What is a divergent bar graph?
back: Bars drawn above and below (or either side of) a central zero line
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: When is a divergent graph used?
back: For data with positive and negative values, such as bipolar scores
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What does a scatter graph show?
back: The relationship between two variables
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: On a scatter graph, which axis is the independent variable plotted on?
back: The x (horizontal) axis
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What does a best fit line on a scatter graph show?
back: The trend of the relationship
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: Through which point should a best fit line pass?
back: The mean point (mean of x, mean of y)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What does a best fit line rising from left to right show?
back: A positive correlation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What does a best fit line falling from left to right show?
back: A negative correlation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: Does a strong correlation on a scatter graph prove that one variable causes the other?
back: No, correlation does not prove causation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: When is a logarithmic scale used on a graph?
back: When data cover a very large range of values
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: On a logarithmic scale, what happens to values with each cycle?
back: They increase tenfold (x10)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What is a semi-logarithmic graph?
back: A graph with one log axis and one normal (arithmetic) axis
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: Which value is impossible to plot on a logarithmic scale?
back: Zero
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What is a triangular graph used for?
back: Three variables that add up to 100%
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: Which classic data set is plotted on a triangular graph in physical geography?
back: Soil or sediment texture (sand, silt and clay)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: How many degrees of a pie chart represent 25% of the total?
back: 90 degrees
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: How do you convert a percentage to degrees for a pie chart?
back: Multiply by 3.6
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What is a proportional divided circle?
back: A pie chart whose circle area is proportional to the total
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: For proportional circles, the circle radius is proportional to what?
back: The square root of the value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: One proportional circle shows 400, another 100. How many times larger is the first circle's radius?
back: 2 times (square root of 4)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What is a dispersion diagram?
back: Individual values plotted as dots along a vertical scale to show spread
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: Which statistics are read easily from a dispersion diagram?
back: The median and interquartile range
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What does a kite diagram show?
back: Abundance or cover of species along a transect
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: Where is a kite diagram commonly used in physical geography fieldwork?
back: Vegetation succession across sand dunes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What does a rose diagram show?
back: Direction and frequency, such as wind direction
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: Besides wind direction, name one use of a rose diagram in geography.
back: Pebble (clast) orientation (also: corrie aspect)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What does a Lorenz curve plot?
back: Cumulative % of a variable against cumulative % of the population
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What does the straight diagonal line on a Lorenz curve graph represent?
back: Perfect equality
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: On a Lorenz curve, what does a curve far from the diagonal show?
back: High inequality (uneven distribution)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: What does a box and whisker plot show?
back: Median, quartiles and range of a data set
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.3 Graphical skills

front: How is the mean calculated?
back: Add all the values and divide by the number of values
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the median?
back: The middle value when data are in rank order
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the mode?
back: The most frequent value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Why is the median often better than the mean for data with extreme values?
back: The median is not affected by outliers
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Which measure of central tendency suits nominal (category) data?
back: The mode
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: what is the mean of 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: what is the median of 2, 4, 6 and 8?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: what is the mode of 4, 6, 6, 6, 9 and 9?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the range?
back: The highest value minus the lowest value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Give one limitation of the range as a measure of dispersion.
back: It is distorted by one extreme value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: what is the range of 12, 3, 27 and 8?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the interquartile range?
back: The upper quartile minus the lower quartile
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What part of a data set does the interquartile range describe?
back: The spread of the middle 50% of values
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Give one strength of the interquartile range over the range.
back: It is not affected by extreme values
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: what is the interquartile range of 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13?
back: 8 (upper quartile 11 minus lower quartile 3)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does standard deviation measure?
back: The average spread of values around the mean
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does a small standard deviation show?
back: Values are clustered closely around the mean
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does a large standard deviation show?
back: Values are widely spread from the mean
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: In the standard deviation formula used on AQA papers, what is divided by n before taking the square root?
back: The sum of (x minus mean) squared
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: In a normal distribution, roughly what percentage of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean?
back: About 68%
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: what is the standard deviation (dividing by n) of 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7 and 9?
back: 2 (mean 5, sum of squared deviations 32, 32/8 = 4, square root 2)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does Spearman's rank correlation test?
back: The strength and direction of the relationship between two variables
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What type of data does Spearman's rank use?
back: Paired data converted to ranks
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the formula for Spearman's rank correlation coefficient?
back: rs = 1 - (6 x sum of d squared) / (n cubed - n)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: In the Spearman's rank formula, what is d?
back: The difference between the two ranks for each pair
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: In the Spearman's rank formula, what is n?
back: The number of pairs of data
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Between which values does Spearman's rank coefficient always lie?
back: -1 and +1
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does a Spearman's rank value of +1 mean?
back: Perfect positive correlation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does a Spearman's rank value of -1 mean?
back: Perfect negative correlation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does a Spearman's rank value close to 0 mean?
back: No correlation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: for 5 pairs with sum of d squared = 4, what is Spearman's rs?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: for 5 pairs with sum of d squared = 40, what is Spearman's rs?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: When ranking, how are tied values ranked?
back: Each gets the average of the ranks they would share
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: ranking 10, 8, 8 and 5 from highest, what rank do the two 8s get?
back: 2.5 each
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: How do you test whether a Spearman's rank result is significant?
back: Compare rs with the critical value for n in a significance table
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: When is a Spearman's rank result significant?
back: When rs (ignoring its sign) is equal to or above the critical value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does the chi-squared test assess?
back: Whether observed frequencies differ significantly from expected frequencies
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the formula for chi-squared?
back: Sum of (O - E) squared / E
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: In the chi-squared formula, what are O and E?
back: Observed and expected frequencies
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What type of data does the chi-squared test need?
back: Frequencies (counts) in categories, not percentages
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: In a chi-squared test, what is the minimum expected frequency usually required in each category?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: How are degrees of freedom found for a chi-squared contingency table?
back: (rows - 1) x (columns - 1)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: How are degrees of freedom found for a one-row chi-squared test with k categories?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: how many degrees of freedom does a 3 row by 4 column chi-squared table have?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: observed counts 30 and 10, expected 20 and 20. What is chi-squared?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the critical value of chi-squared at 1 degree of freedom and 0.05 significance?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: When is a chi-squared result significant?
back: When it is equal to or above the critical value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does the Mann-Whitney U test assess?
back: Whether two independent samples differ significantly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the formula for U1 in the Mann-Whitney U test?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: In the Mann-Whitney U formula, what is R1?
back: The sum of the ranks of sample 1
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: In the Mann-Whitney U test, which U value is compared with the critical value?
back: The smaller of U1 and U2
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: When is a Mann-Whitney U result significant?
back: When the smaller U is equal to or below the critical value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: two samples of 5, sample 1 rank sum R1 = 20. What is U1?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does nearest neighbour analysis measure?
back: Whether a point pattern is clustered, random or regular
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the formula for the nearest neighbour index (Rn)?
back: Rn = 2 x mean distance x square root of (n / area)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What nearest neighbour index value shows a perfectly clustered pattern?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What nearest neighbour index value shows a random pattern?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What nearest neighbour index value shows a perfectly regular (uniform) pattern?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: mean nearest neighbour distance 1 km, 25 points, area 100 km squared. What is Rn?
back: 1.0, a random pattern
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: Worked example: mean nearest neighbour distance 0.1 km, 25 points, area 100 km squared. What is Rn?
back: 0.1, a clustered pattern
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does the Gini coefficient measure?
back: Inequality in a distribution, such as income
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What Gini coefficient value means perfect equality?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What Gini coefficient value means perfect inequality?
back: 1 (or 100 when written as a percentage)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: From which graph is the Gini coefficient derived?
back: The Lorenz curve
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is a null hypothesis?
back: A statement that there is no significant relationship or difference
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is an alternative hypothesis?
back: A statement that there is a significant relationship or difference
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What happens to the null hypothesis when a test result is significant?
back: It is rejected
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does a significance level of 0.05 mean?
back: A 5% probability the result occurred by chance (95% confidence)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What does a significance level of 0.01 mean?
back: A 1% probability the result occurred by chance (99% confidence)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is the minimum significance level usually accepted in geography?
back: 0.05 (95% confidence)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What are degrees of freedom in a statistical test?
back: The number of values free to vary, used to choose the critical value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is a critical value?
back: The value from a table that a test result must reach to be significant
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.4 Statistical skills

front: What is a GIS (geographical information system)?
back: A computer system to capture, store, analyse and display located data
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: How does a GIS organise different data sets?
back: As layers that can be overlaid
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: What is remote sensing?
back: Collecting data about the Earth from a distance, such as by satellite
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: Name one source of remotely sensed data.
back: Satellite images (also: aerial photographs, drone images)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: What is crowd sourcing of data?
back: Collecting data from large numbers of the public, often online
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: Give one limitation of crowd-sourced data.
back: Its accuracy is hard to check
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: What is big data?
back: Extremely large data sets, such as phone location data, analysed by computer
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: What is an electronic database?
back: An organised store of data held on a computer that can be searched
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: What is GPS used for in fieldwork?
back: Recording the exact location of data points
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: What is the difference between raster and vector data in GIS?
back: Raster is a grid of cells, vector uses points, lines and polygons
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: Give one strength of using ICT to produce graphs and statistics.
back: It is fast and reduces calculation errors
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Geographical skills and fieldwork::Geographical skills checklist::3.4.2.5 ICT skills

front: In systems theory, what is a system?
back: A set of linked stores (components) with flows (transfers) of matter or energy between them

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: What is the term for a system that receives inputs from, and loses outputs to, its surroundings?
back: An open system
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: What is the term for a system where energy crosses the boundary but matter does not?
back: A closed system
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: At the global scale, is the water cycle an open or a closed system?
back: Closed (no water enters or leaves; energy does)
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: Is a drainage basin an open or a closed system?
back: Open (water enters as precipitation and leaves as runoff and evapotranspiration)
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: At the global scale, is the carbon cycle an open or a closed system?
back: Closed (carbon is recycled within the Earth system)
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: In a system, what is an input?
back: Matter or energy that enters the system from outside
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: In a system, what is an output?
back: Matter or energy that leaves the system
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: In a system, what is a store?
back: A part of the system where matter or energy is held for a time
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: In a system, what is a flow (transfer)?
back: The movement of matter or energy from one store to another
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: Which energy source drives evaporation and most of the water cycle?
back: Solar energy (the sun)
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: Which force drives water downhill through a drainage basin and makes precipitation fall?
back: Gravity
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: What is the term for a system state where inputs and outputs balance so the stores stay roughly constant over time?
back: Dynamic equilibrium
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: Why is dynamic equilibrium called "dynamic"?
back: Flows keep happening, but the overall balance between them stays the same
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: What type of feedback reverses a change and returns a system towards equilibrium?
back: Negative feedback
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: What type of feedback amplifies a change and moves a system further from equilibrium?
back: Positive feedback
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: In a negative carbon feedback, how does more atmospheric CO2 lead to more carbon being stored?
back: Plants photosynthesise faster and take up more CO2 (CO2 fertilisation)
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: Which type of event can suddenly upset the dynamic equilibrium of a drainage basin?
back: An extreme event such as a storm, flood or drought
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: What is the term for a critical point beyond which a system changes to a new state and does not return?
back: A tipping point (threshold)
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: What is the term for the area that a system covers, which separates it from its surroundings?
back: The system boundary
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: In a drainage basin system, which feature forms the boundary?
back: The watershed
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: In systems terms, what is a sink?
back: A store that takes in more of a substance (e.g. carbon) than it releases
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: In systems terms, what is a source?
back: A store that releases more of a substance than it takes in
point: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

front: Which of the four water stores (lithosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere) holds the most water?
back: The hydrosphere (the oceans)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Which store holds most of Earth's fresh water?
back: The cryosphere (ice sheets and glaciers)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: After ice, which store holds the next largest share of Earth's fresh water?
back: Groundwater (in the lithosphere)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Which of the four main water stores holds the smallest volume of water?
back: The atmosphere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the cryosphere?
back: The parts of Earth where water is frozen (ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, snow)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the lithosphere's water store mainly made of?
back: Groundwater and soil water held in rocks and soil
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is residence time in the water cycle?
back: The average time a water molecule spends in a store
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Why does water in the atmosphere have a much shorter residence time than water in the oceans?
back: The atmosphere's store is tiny compared with the rapid flows of evaporation and precipitation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is evaporation?
back: The change of liquid water into water vapour
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for the energy absorbed when water evaporates, which is released again on condensation?
back: Latent heat
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Which factor increases evaporation by removing saturated air from above a water surface?
back: Wind
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Why does evaporation increase as air temperature rises?
back: Warm air holds more water vapour and gives more energy for evaporation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is condensation?
back: The change of water vapour into liquid water droplets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the dew point?
back: The temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What do tiny particles such as dust, salt and smoke provide for cloud formation?
back: Condensation nuclei for water droplets to form on
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for cooling of rising air caused by its expansion at lower pressure, with no heat lost to surroundings?
back: Adiabatic cooling
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: At what rate does unsaturated (dry) air cool as it rises?
back: About 9.8°C per 1,000 m (the dry adiabatic lapse rate)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Why does saturated air cool more slowly than dry air as it rises?
back: Condensation releases latent heat, which partly offsets the cooling
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for the rate at which temperature falls with height in still air?
back: The environmental lapse rate
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: When rising air stays warmer than the air around it, what is the atmosphere said to be?
back: Unstable (air keeps rising, forming towering clouds)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for rainfall caused by the ground heating air, which rises, cools and condenses?
back: Convectional rainfall
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for rainfall caused when moist air is forced to rise over high ground?
back: Relief (orographic) rainfall
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for rainfall caused when warm air is forced to rise over colder, denser air?
back: Frontal rainfall
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for the drier area on the downwind (leeward) side of mountains?
back: A rain shadow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Why is the leeward side of mountains drier?
back: Descending air warms, so water does not condense
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Which type of rainfall gives the UK most of its rain, through mid-latitude depressions?
back: Frontal rainfall
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is sublimation?
back: The change of ice directly into water vapour without melting
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for water vapour changing directly into ice, as in frost?
back: Deposition
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: In a glacier, what is accumulation?
back: Inputs of snow and ice to the glacier store
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: In a glacier, what is ablation?
back: Loss of ice by melting, sublimation or calving
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is calving?
back: Blocks of ice breaking off the front of a glacier or ice sheet into water
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: In which season does ablation usually exceed accumulation on glaciers?
back: Summer
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What happens to global sea level when ice sheets grow in a glacial period?
back: It falls, as water is moved from the oceans into the cryosphere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is a drainage basin?
back: The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is a watershed?
back: The boundary (usually a ridge of high land) between two drainage basins
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is a confluence?
back: The point where two rivers join
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is a tributary?
back: A smaller stream that joins a larger river
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the main input to a drainage basin?
back: Precipitation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is interception?
back: Precipitation caught and held by vegetation before it reaches the ground
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for intercepted water that evaporates from leaves without reaching the ground?
back: Interception loss
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for water flowing down the trunks and stems of plants to the ground?
back: Stemflow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for water dripping from leaves to the ground?
back: Throughfall
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Why is interception lower in winter in deciduous woodland?
back: The trees have lost their leaves
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is surface storage?
back: Water held on the ground surface in puddles, ponds and lakes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is infiltration?
back: The movement of water from the surface into the soil
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the infiltration capacity of a soil?
back: The maximum rate at which water can soak into the soil
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Which unit is infiltration rate usually measured in?
back: Millimetres per hour (mm/hr)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Why do sandy soils have a higher infiltration capacity than clay soils?
back: They have larger pore spaces between particles
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is soil water storage?
back: Water held in the pores of the soil
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is throughflow?
back: Water moving downslope through the soil towards the river
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is percolation?
back: Water moving down from the soil into the rock below
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is groundwater?
back: Water stored in the pores and joints of rock below the water table
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the water table?
back: The upper level of the saturated zone in the ground
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is an aquifer?
back: A permeable rock that stores and transmits groundwater (e.g. chalk or sandstone)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for the slow flow of groundwater through rock to the river?
back: Groundwater flow (baseflow)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is groundwater recharge?
back: Refilling of groundwater stores by water percolating down
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is channel storage?
back: Water held in the river channel itself
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is channel flow?
back: The movement of water along the river channel
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is overland flow?
back: Water flowing across the ground surface towards a river
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for overland flow caused when rainfall intensity exceeds the infiltration capacity?
back: Infiltration-excess (Hortonian) overland flow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for overland flow caused when the soil is already full of water?
back: Saturation-excess overland flow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is runoff in a drainage basin?
back: All the water leaving the basin as river flow (surface and subsurface)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is transpiration?
back: Loss of water vapour from plants through pores (stomata) in their leaves
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is evapotranspiration?
back: The combined loss of water by evaporation and transpiration
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for the amount of evapotranspiration that would happen if water supply were unlimited?
back: Potential evapotranspiration
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the water balance equation for a drainage basin?
back: P = Q + E ± ΔS (precipitation = runoff + evapotranspiration ± change in storage)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: In the water balance equation, what does Q stand for?
back: Runoff (river discharge)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for a period when evapotranspiration exceeds precipitation and plants draw on soil water?
back: Soil moisture utilisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for the shortage of soil water when evapotranspiration has used up the soil store?
back: Soil moisture deficit
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for autumn and winter rain refilling the soil water store?
back: Soil moisture recharge
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for a period when soil is full and extra precipitation becomes runoff?
back: Water surplus
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: In the UK, in which season is a soil moisture deficit most likely?
back: Summer
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is river discharge?
back: The volume of water passing a point on a river per second
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: In which unit is river discharge measured?
back: Cumecs (cubic metres per second)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How is discharge calculated?
back: Cross-sectional area × velocity
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is a flood (storm) hydrograph?
back: A graph of river discharge over time after a rainfall event
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is lag time on a flood hydrograph?
back: The time between peak rainfall and peak discharge
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the rising limb of a hydrograph?
back: The part of the graph where discharge increases after the rain
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the falling (recession) limb of a hydrograph?
back: The part of the graph where discharge decreases after the peak
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is baseflow?
back: The normal flow of a river, fed mainly by groundwater
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is stormflow (quickflow)?
back: Discharge from overland flow and fast throughflow after rain
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is peak discharge?
back: The highest discharge reached after a storm
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is bankfull discharge?
back: The discharge at which the river just fills its channel (any more and it floods)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is a "flashy" hydrograph?
back: One with a short lag time, steep rising limb and high peak
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What does a subdued (flat) hydrograph show?
back: A long lag time and a low peak discharge
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is antecedent rainfall?
back: Rain that fell before a storm, which may already have saturated the ground
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does saturated ground from antecedent rainfall affect a flood hydrograph?
back: Less infiltration, so more overland flow, a shorter lag time and higher peak
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does a circular drainage basin affect lag time compared with an elongated one?
back: Shorter lag time, as water from all parts reaches the river at a similar time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does a small drainage basin affect lag time?
back: Shorter lag time, as water has less distance to travel
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is drainage density?
back: The total length of streams per unit area of the basin (km per km²)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does a high drainage density affect a flood hydrograph?
back: Water reaches the main river faster, giving a shorter lag time and higher peak
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How do steep slopes affect a flood hydrograph?
back: Faster overland flow, so a shorter lag time and higher peak
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does impermeable rock such as granite or clay affect a flood hydrograph?
back: Little percolation, so more overland flow and a flashier hydrograph
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does permeable rock such as chalk affect a flood hydrograph?
back: Water percolates to groundwater, giving a long lag time and low peak
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does dense forest cover affect a flood hydrograph?
back: More interception and transpiration, so a longer lag time and lower peak
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does urbanisation affect a flood hydrograph?
back: Impermeable surfaces and drains speed runoff, so lag time falls and peak rises
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How do storm drains in towns affect river response?
back: They carry rainwater quickly to rivers, shortening lag time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does frozen ground affect a flood hydrograph?
back: It acts as an impermeable surface, increasing overland flow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Why can rapid snowmelt cause flooding?
back: Large volumes of water are released at once, often onto frozen or saturated ground
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does high rainfall intensity affect overland flow?
back: Rain arrives faster than the infiltration capacity, so overland flow increases
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for an approach that works with natural processes (e.g. leaky dams, tree planting) to cut flood peaks?
back: Natural flood management
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does ploughing up and down a slope affect runoff?
back: Furrows act as channels, speeding overland flow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does soil compaction by heavy machinery or livestock affect the water cycle?
back: It reduces infiltration and increases overland flow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does field drainage on farmland affect a hydrograph?
back: Water reaches rivers faster, shortening lag time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does irrigation affect the water cycle?
back: It removes water from rivers or groundwater and raises evaporation from fields
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does deforestation affect a drainage basin's water cycle?
back: Less interception and transpiration, so more runoff and higher flood risk
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does afforestation affect a drainage basin's water cycle?
back: More interception and transpiration, so less and slower runoff
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is water abstraction?
back: Removing water from rivers, lakes or groundwater for human use
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What happens to the water table if groundwater is abstracted faster than it is recharged?
back: It falls
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How do reservoirs and dams affect a river's discharge downstream?
back: They store water and regulate flow, reducing flood peaks and low flows
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How do seasonal changes in the UK affect river discharge?
back: Discharge is usually higher in winter (more rain, less evapotranspiration)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does a storm event change drainage basin stores in the short term?
back: It fills soil, surface and channel stores and raises discharge
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What happens to river discharge when a drought lowers soil and groundwater stores?
back: Discharge falls as baseflow is reduced
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Which long-term natural change moved large amounts of water from the oceans into ice stores?
back: Glacial periods (ice ages)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: How does global warming affect the cryosphere store?
back: It shrinks, as ice melts and water moves into the oceans
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Why does warmer air lead to more intense rainfall?
back: Warmer air holds more water vapour (about 7% more per 1°C)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: What is the term for a natural climate pattern of warming in the eastern Pacific that alters rainfall patterns around the world?
back: El Niño (ENSO)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.2 The water cycle

front: Which of the carbon stores is by far the largest?
back: The lithosphere (sedimentary rocks such as limestone, and fossil fuels)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: Which is the second largest carbon store after the lithosphere?
back: The oceans (hydrosphere), mostly as dissolved inorganic carbon in the deep ocean
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: In which form is most carbon in the oceans stored?
back: Dissolved inorganic carbon (bicarbonate and carbonate ions)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: In which form is most carbon in the atmosphere stored?
back: Carbon dioxide (CO2), with smaller amounts of methane (CH4)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: Where is carbon stored in the cryosphere?
back: In permafrost soils and in ice (as trapped gas)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: Where is carbon stored in the biosphere?
back: In living plants and animals and in dead organic matter
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: On land, which holds more carbon: soils or vegetation?
back: Soils
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: Why do cold high-latitude soils store large amounts of carbon?
back: Low temperatures slow decomposition, so organic matter builds up (e.g. peat)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is peat?
back: Partly decomposed plant matter that builds up in waterlogged, acidic, cold conditions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is photosynthesis?
back: Plants use sunlight to turn CO2 and water into glucose and oxygen
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
back: Carbon dioxide + water (+ light) → glucose + oxygen
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is respiration?
back: Organisms break down glucose for energy, releasing CO2 and water
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is decomposition?
back: The breakdown of dead organic matter by bacteria, fungi and detritivores, releasing CO2
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What are organisms such as worms and woodlice that feed on dead organic matter called?
back: Detritivores
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: Why is decomposition fastest in hot, wet climates?
back: Warmth and moisture increase microbial activity
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What gas does decomposition release in waterlogged, oxygen-poor conditions?
back: Methane (CH4)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is combustion?
back: Burning of organic matter or fossil fuels, releasing CO2 to the atmosphere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is carbon sequestration?
back: The capture and long-term storage of carbon from the atmosphere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is net primary productivity (NPP)?
back: The carbon fixed by photosynthesis minus the carbon lost by plant respiration
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is gross primary productivity (GPP)?
back: The total carbon fixed by plants through photosynthesis
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is the term for the gradual change in plant communities over time on a site?
back: Succession
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is a sere?
back: One complete sequence of succession from bare ground to climax community
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: How does carbon storage change as a sere develops?
back: It increases, as biomass and soil organic matter build up
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is the final, stable stage of succession called?
back: The climax community
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: At the plant scale, where does a plant store the carbon it fixes?
back: In its leaves, stems, trunk and roots (biomass)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: How does carbon pass from plants to animals?
back: Animals eat plants (consumption along food chains)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What is the term for dead leaves and plant material on the soil surface, a carbon store?
back: Litter
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: Which biome has the largest carbon store in its vegetation?
back: Tropical rainforest

back: Cold slows growth, but it also slows decomposition so carbon builds up in soil
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

front: What weak acid forms when CO2 dissolves in rainwater?
back: Carbonic acid
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

back: Shells and skeletons of marine organisms (calcium carbonate) settle and are compressed
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle

back: Dead organic matter is buried and compressed without oxygen over millions of years
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Water and carbon cycles::3.1.1.3 The carbon cycle
